facts: JanusDDG is a model developed for predicting sequence-based protein stability.
The model utilizes a two-fronts multi-head attention mechanism.
The research team is from the Computational Biomedicine Unit at the University of Turin, Italy.
The goal of the research team is to enhance the accuracy of protein stability predictions.
JanusDDG is a deep learning framework that predicts the change in free energy (ΔΔG) caused by mutations.
JanusDDG utilizes protein language model (PLM) embeddings and a bidirectional cross-attention transformer.
JanusDDG achieves state-of-the-art accuracy in predicting ΔΔG from sequence data.
The code for JanusDDG is available at https://github.com/compbiomed-unito/JanusDDG.

The study quantifies protein stability using the change in Gibbs free energy (∆∆𝐺). A positive ∆∆𝐺 indicates a stabilizing mutation. The research introduces JanusDDG, a deep learning model for predicting ∆∆𝐺. JanusDDG incorporates antisymmetry and transitivity to enhance prediction accuracy.
JanusDDG is a sequence-based model for predicting protein stability.
JanusDDG incorporates thermodynamic principles such as antisymmetry and transitivity.
The model utilizes bidirectional cross-attention to process the entire protein sequence.
The performance of JanusDDG is evaluated on established benchmark datasets.
The JanusDDG model enforces antisymmetry through a siamese neural network architecture.
The Pearson correlation coefficient for antisymmetric behavior in JanusDDG is -1.00.
JanusDDG was fine-tuned with an additional loss function to enhance transitivity.
Evaluations on the S669 test set showed improved transitivity in the JanusDDG model.
JanusDDG was evaluated using datasets with less than 25% sequence identity to the training set.
The model was tested on three primary datasets: S669, S461, and S96.
JanusDDG showed strong performance metrics in identifying stabilizing mutations using the S461 dataset.
The model revealed no significant performance differences based on the distance between mutated residues when predicting double mutations.
JanusDDG is a new sequence-based deep learning model for predicting protein stability changes due to mutations.
JanusDDG uses a bidirectional cross-attention architecture combined with protein language model embeddings.
The model excels in predicting the effects of multiple mutations compared to existing models.
The authors suggest future validation of JanusDDG across a wider range of mutations and structural classes.
The S669 dataset includes 1338 single-site mutations across 95 proteins.
The S461 dataset contains 461 mutations from 48 proteins.
The PTmul-NR dataset is designed for multi-point mutations and contains 82 variants across 14 proteins.
The S2450 dataset is a refined version of S2648 and serves as the primary training resource.
The Pearson correlation coefficient measures the linear relationship between two variables.
Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) quantifies the average squared difference between predicted and observed values.
The Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC) is used to evaluate classification performance.
The Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve includes the Area Under the Curve (AUC) to assess overall performance.
The protein embeddings were derived from ESM2 with 650 million parameters.
The differences between wild-type and mutated protein embeddings are primarily localized around the mutation site.
The authors used the non-absolute difference between the two embeddings to predict ∆∆𝐺.
The results indicated a high Pearson correlation on both training and test sets.
The JanusDDG model architecture integrates protein language models with a Cross-Attention mechanism.
The model predicts protein stability based solely on sequence data, regardless of mutation count.
It employs two 1D convolutions to identify sequence patterns and reduce dimensionality.
The output is processed by a linear layer to produce the final ∆∆𝐺 value.
JanusDDG underwent training in two phases: a main training phase and a fine-tuning phase.
The main training utilized the S2450 dataset with 300 epochs determined through 5-fold cross-validation.
The fine-tuning phase aimed to enhance performance regarding multiple mutations and the transitivity property of ∆∆𝐺.
The optimal epoch for fine-tuning was selected as 28 based on validation with the M28 dataset.
The Bidirectional Transformer model used 8 Transformer heads.
The authors performed 5-fold cross-validation resulting in 300 training epochs.
JanusDDG achieved a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.69 on the S669 dataset.
The mean squared error for JanusDDG on the S96 dataset was 2.10.
